notes.quote: וַ⁠יִּשְׁלַ֗ח אֲבִימֶ֨לֶךְ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ גְּרָ֔ר וַ⁠יִּקַּ֖ח אֶת־שָׂרָֽה
notes.text: The city of Gerar was the Philistines’ capital city where King Abimelech ruled from (Genesis 21:2, 32; 26:1). or [So one day King Abimelech, who ruled the Philistines from the city of Gerar, had Sarah brought to him to be his wife]

For some languages it is necessary to use an honorific title for a king each time (or most of the time) that he is referred to by name, in order to show him proper respect. Do what is best in your language throughout this chapter.
It may be more natural to put this time phrase earlier in this sentence and say, “But that night God appeared to King Abimelech in a dream …” or [by night]

God is using the present tense to describe something that is going to happen in the future in order to warn that the event could happen soon. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use the future tense. Make sure that the way you translate this clause does not make it sound like King Abimelech is already dead.
Consider what is the best way in your language to introduce this background information.

King Abimelech uses a rhetorical question here to express his desperate concern. Abimelech is saying in a dramatic way that if God kills him, he will destroy the innocent nation that Abimelech leads as their king. Make sure in your translation that he sounds humble and not angry or rude.
or [with pure motives]

notes.topic: in the innocence of my hands
notes.text: Abimilech’s statement, **in the innocence of my hands**, means that he was not aware of any wrongdoing in his actions. If you use an exclamation point here in your translation, make sure it does not mean that King Abimelech is angry or being rude; rather, he is desperate.
or [with pure motives]
In the Hebrew text, **I** is an emphatic pronoun. Try to communicate that emphasis in a natural way in your translation. or [In fact, I am the one who prevented you from sinning against me]
Also, for some languages it may be better to change the order of these clauses and say, “I am the one who did not allow you to touch her so that you would not sin against me.” or [do anything to her]
The phrase **all who belong to you** refers to King Abimelech’s people, whom he referred to in verse 4. Make sure that is clear in your translation. or [I will surely kill you and all your people!]
or [He told them everything that had happened]

Consider what is the best way in your language to refer to King Abimelech’s servants at each point in this verse. or [When they heard that, they were very afraid that God would kill them] or [As soon as they heard that, the men were very afraid of what might happen next]

notes.quote: וַ⁠יִּקְרָ֨א אֲבִימֶ֜לֶךְ לְ⁠אַבְרָהָ֗ם וַ⁠יֹּ֨אמֶר ל֜⁠וֹ מֶֽה־עָשִׂ֤יתָ לָּ֨⁠נוּ֙ וּ⁠מֶֽה־חָטָ֣אתִי לָ֔⁠ךְ כִּֽי־הֵבֵ֧אתָ עָלַ֛⁠י וְ⁠עַל־מַמְלַכְתִּ֖⁠י חֲטָאָ֣ה גְדֹלָ֑ה מַעֲשִׂים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹא־יֵֽעָשׂ֔וּ עָשִׂ֖יתָ עִמָּדִֽ⁠י
notes.text: In this verse, the pronouns **him** and **you** refer to **Abraham**, while the pronouns **I**, **me**, and **us** refer to **Abimilech**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers.
Make sure your punctuation here fits with how you translate this rhetorical question. or [you have caused me and the kingdom that I rule to be guilty of sinning terribly!]

For some languages it is more natural here to omit this quote margin, because the same person is still talking to the same person. However, the words emphasize what King Abimelech says next and may indicate that there was a pause between what he said in verse 9 and in verse 10.

notes.topic: or [What were your reasons for doing]
notes.text: or [What were your reasons for doing]
You may need to translate this phrase in different ways, depending on the context. or [wherever you want]

notes.topic: Coins did not exist at that time
notes.text: Coins did not exist at that time. Rather, people paid each other with shekels of silver or gold shekels, which was a weight measurement. A thousand shekels of silver was about 25 pounds (11.5 kilos) of silver. Many translation teams like to keep the same numbers that are in the Hebrew text in their translation, and then in a footnote give the equivalent amount in their own currency. Other teams put the equivalent amount in the text and put the literal phrase in a footnote. or [I have given your brother 1,000 pieces of silver]

notes.quote: לָ⁠ךְ֙ כְּס֣וּת עֵינַ֔יִם לְ⁠כֹ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר אִתָּ֑⁠ךְ
notes.text: The phrase **a covering of the eyes** is an idiom which means that King Abimelech’s payment to Abraham “covered” (that is, “protected”) Sarah’s good reputation and showed that she was innocent. or [to show to everyone that you are an honorable woman]

notes.quote: עָצֹ֤ר עָצַר֙ & בְּעַ֥ד כָּל־רֶ֖חֶם לְ⁠בֵ֣ית אֲבִימֶ֑לֶךְ
notes.text: Consider again how often you need to use the honorific title “King” with Abimelech’s name in this chapter in your language.
or [to punish him for taking]

For some languages, it may be more natural to change the order of the clauses in this sentence (which begins in verse 17) and say, “Before this, Yahweh had completely closed up every womb in the household of King Abimelech because he had taken Abraham’s wife Sarah. Then Abraham prayed …” If the order is changed, it will be necessary to combine these two verses and to put the verse numbers “17–18” in front of the sentence. Some translation teams have decided that they will never combine verses like that. Other teams have decided that occasionally it is acceptable to do that if it makes the meaning clearer.
